name: Prize crossword No 22,845
preamble: Solutions must be entered in the diagram jigsaw-wise, wherever they will go. Those to A, C, R and S are acrosses; those to D, W and N are downs.

clue.text: False tongue gives information at the top

blocks.note: news is information about recent events
the peak is the topmost point

explanation.surface: A lying tongue passes on information from the people in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: NEWSPEAK is the deceptive official language of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four; 'tongue' here means a language, not the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's invented language exists to distort meaning and limit thought, so it is a deliberately dishonest language.

clue.text: Vic's game? You move as shown by dice's score

definitions.text: You move as shown by dice's score

blocks.note: first meaning: Vic is short for Victor Ludorum, the 'winner of the games' at a school sports day, whose Latin for games begins with these letters

blocks.clueFragment: You move as shown by dice's score
blocks.note: second meaning: a children's board game where counters move by the throw of a die

explanation.walkthrough: Victor Ludorum is the title given to the overall champion at a British school sports day; Latin ludus means game, so Vic's game is a playful nod to his title.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludo is a simple race board game in which players advance counters according to their throws of a die.

clue.text: Peter (in opera) made poor Tom so black

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of the fisherman who is the title character of Britten's opera
second meaning: in Kingsley's The Water-Babies, the master sweep whose boy Tom is always covered in soot

explanation.walkthrough: Two literary characters share one surname: Britten's tragic fisherman, and the cruel chimney sweep who employs little Tom in Charles Kingsley's The Water-Babies.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to the title character of Britten's opera and to the sooty sweep master in Kingsley's children's novel.

clue.text: Shows cowardice, not that in Manx display

definitions.note: the clue phrase is a verb phrase; the answer is a noun for yellow colouring

indicators.note: to display is to set out or arrange for show, so the letters are laid out afresh

blocks.note: the word you use when you mean not that one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone shows cowardice by refusing to join a show on the Isle of Man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not that' is a riddle: the opposite of that is this. Yellow is slang for cowardly, and the answer is the technical word for abnormal yellow colouring.
explanation.definitionFit: Being yellow is an idiom for cowardice, and xanthism is the condition of being unusually yellow in colour, so it puns on showing cowardice.

clue.text: Transparencies that save things from decay

definitions.note: a relative clause describing what the answer does; the answer is a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: read as two words, things you can see through, one liquid and one solid
second meaning: a sodium silicate solution once used to preserve eggs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Transparencies' suggests photographic slides, but it means two see-through substances named together; the whole is an old egg preservative.
explanation.definitionFit: Water glass, a sodium silicate solution, was traditionally used to coat and preserve eggs, keeping them from going off.

clue.text: Very old and young heads time at sea

definitions.note: the answer is a noun for a sea journey; the clue phrase is adverbial

indicators.note: the head of a word is its front, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: opening letters of the two words
opening letter of the word
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Old and young passengers alike spend time on a sea journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heads' looks like a verb about leading, but it asks for the first letters of the three preceding words.
explanation.definitionFit: A voyage is a long journey made by ship, the period someone spends travelling across the sea.

clue.text: Wanted some sheets to infiltrate the left

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to get inside a group, so one piece slips inside another

blocks.note: a quire is a set of 24 or 25 sheets of paper
red is the colour of the political left

explanation.surface: Someone sought paper to slip into a left-wing organisation, perhaps to spread propaganda.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the left' is political, not a direction: Reds are left-wingers.
explanation.definitionFit: Required and wanted are synonyms in the sense of needed or demanded, as in 'your presence is wanted'.

clue.text: Resembling Hamlet as applied to Bacon?

blocks.note: first meaning: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark
second meaning: the label on a well-known kind of cured pork from Denmark

explanation.walkthrough: The capital B and the Shakespeare play point to Francis Bacon, whom some claim wrote Shakespeare; really it is breakfast bacon, which Britain imports from Denmark.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective for things from Denmark describes both the Shakespearean prince and a popular imported British breakfast meat.

clue.text: A fighting girl, the longest on the map

blocks.note: first meaning: one of a legendary race of women warriors
second meaning: the South American river, by some measures the world's longest

explanation.walkthrough: 'the longest on the map' leaves the noun unstated; it means the longest river.
explanation.definitionFit: Greek legend tells of a nation of female warriors, and the great South American river was named after them.

clue.text: A capital in bondage to Slovenes

indicators.note: something in bondage is held captive, so the letters are held within the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A European capital has fallen under the control of Slovenes.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles 'to' and 'Slovenes'; Slovenia's capital is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Oslo is the capital city of Norway, one example of a nation's seat of government.

clue.text: Please watch this space, or on the line you'll drop

definitions.note: describes the hazard the answer warns of rather than naming it

blocks.note: first meaning: literally, take care over the space in front of you
second meaning: the London Underground warning about the space between train and platform edge, lest you fall onto the track

explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch this space' sounds like 'more news soon', but the space is the gap at a Tube platform; the London Underground recording warns passengers to step carefully over it.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous London Underground recorded warning asks passengers to beware the space between the train door and the platform.

clue.text: S lady's nag takes in part-sozzled back

definitions.note: the answer to the clue lettered S in the original jigsaw, SHINGLES

indicators.note: to take something in is to admit it inside, so one piece goes within another
going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: the possessive pronoun for a woman
to nag is to pester
the first part of the word

explanation.surface: A woman's horse comes back half drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: In the original jigsaw each clue had a letter, and S was SHINGLES; nag means pester, not horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Herpes zoster is the medical name for shingles, the painful rash caused by reactivated chickenpox virus.

clue.text: Peck-picker loved Dickensian flanked by Queens

indicators.note: to be flanked is to have something on each side, so one piece sits between two others

blocks.note: a pet is a favourite, someone loved
ER (Elizabeth Regina) twice, one for each queen
Pip is the hero of Dickens's Great Expectations

explanation.surface: A woodpecker-like bird adored by a Dickens character sits between two royal ladies.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the standard crossword Queen. The tongue-twister says Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery tongue-twister, this character gathered a peck, an old dry measure, of pickled peppers.

clue.text: Bone, broken leg's, makes tiles from stones on shore

indicators.note: a broken thing is smashed out of shape, so the letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: the shin bone, or tibia
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone with a broken leg turns beach pebbles into tiles.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer has two senses here, wooden roof tiles and the loose pebbles of a beach.
explanation.definitionFit: Shingles are thin wooden roofing tiles, and shingle is the mass of small rounded pebbles found on a beach.

clue.text: Equipment numbered by small carnivore

blocks.note: kit is a set of equipment
a number, here ten

explanation.surface: Gear is labelled with numbers by a little meat-eating animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'numbered' simply stands for a number, and the number needed is ten.
explanation.definitionFit: A young cat is a little animal, and cats, being meat-eaters, belong to the order Carnivora.

clue.text: Leave land when telly prize superb is heard

indicators.note: what is heard is taken in by ear, so the spoken form matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: an Emmy is an American television award
great means superb

explanation.surface: A TV star leaves the country after news of a top award breaks.
explanation.walkthrough: Say EMMY GREAT quickly and it matches the answer's pronunciation. Telly is British slang for television.
explanation.definitionFit: To emigrate is to leave your own country to settle permanently in another one.

clue.text: This strike must be the devil to perform

blocks.note: an imp is a little devil
to act is to perform

explanation.surface: A complaint about an industrial walkout that will be hellishly difficult to stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strike' suggests a walkout; here it is a blow or collision.
explanation.definitionFit: An impact is the forceful collision of one thing against another, a blow or hit.

clue.text: Three skirts like ancient city with a store

indicators.note: to skirt is to go round the edge, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: a trey is a three at cards or dice
as means like
Ur of the Chaldees, the crossword's favourite old city

explanation.surface: Three women in skirts resemble an ancient city that had a market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skirts' looks like clothing, but it is a verb meaning goes around.
explanation.definitionFit: A treasury is a place where valuables or funds are kept, a repository of riches.

clue.text: The man from Auntie qualified by note

blocks.note: surface reading: a relative's visitor; setter's reading: Auntie is the BBC's nickname, so a famous BBC executive
setter's reading: his surname opens with the name of a Japanese banknote

explanation.walkthrough: Auntie (or Auntie Beeb) is a British nickname for the BBC. Alan Yentob was a long-serving BBC executive, and his name begins with the Japanese currency.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Yentob was a senior BBC executive and presenter for decades, so he is a man from the corporation.

clue.text: A value for some floor of rail bereft

indicators.note: to be bereft is to have been deprived of something, so letters are lost

blocks.note: a quarry tile is an unglazed tile used for some floors
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: Someone prices a floor that has had its railing removed.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the railway abbreviation from the middle of the flooring tile. 'for some' hints that a quartile marks off a quarter of the data.
explanation.definitionFit: In statistics a quartile is one of three values dividing ordered data into four equal parts.

clue.text: Blue with another lacking potency

indicators.note: making something other turns it into a different form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
split into two words: only the first supplies letters

explanation.surface: Feeling down alongside a partner who is impotent.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'another' as 'an other': the first part joins the colour, and 'other' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unable lacks the power or capacity to do something, which is what lacking potency means.

clue.text: See 12
Belt holding such as ram and goat

definitions.text: holding such as ram and goat
definitions.note: describes what the answer contains rather than naming it

blocks.note: first meaning: a band, here the band of sky along the sun's yearly path

blocks.clueFragment: holding such as ram and goat
blocks.note: second meaning: the set of star signs, which includes Aries and Capricorn

explanation.walkthrough: The animals are star signs, not farm stock; astronomers describe this band of sky as a belt.
explanation.definitionFit: The astrological band of twelve constellations along the sun's path includes Aries the ram and Capricorn the goat.

clue.text: About Z7, boy: done so measure's taken

blocks.note: ca, circa, means about
the seventh sign of the zodiac, Z being the clue lettered Z in the original jigsaw
Ted is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A boy's tailoring is finished once his measurements are taken.
explanation.walkthrough: Counting from Aries, Libra is the seventh sign of the zodiac; Z7 means the seventh item in the answer to Z.
explanation.definitionFit: An instrument is calibrated when it has been adjusted and checked so that its readings measure accurately.

clue.text: Cracks put together, judges seek to storm

indicators.note: a storm throws things into turmoil, so the letters are tossed into new order

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation for judge, twice for the plural
taken as written

explanation.surface: Judges want to attack after the cracks in a case are pieced together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracks' means wisecracks, and two of them are wanted, one for each light.
explanation.definitionFit: A crack is a witty remark, and both answer words are everyday synonyms for a funny quip.

clue.text: See 24 across
Able to speak with ease, is left unstirred

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so the letters come out in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written
split after its second letter: only the front supplies letters

explanation.surface: A smooth talker stays calm and undisturbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unstirred' must be split: its first two letters join the fodder, and the rest is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A fluent speaker expresses themselves smoothly and readily, without hesitation, especially in a language.

clue.text: Spelling deficiency in titled chap

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a lack is a deficiency
Bart is short for baronet, a hereditary title

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spelling' suggests orthography, but it means casting spells, magic.
explanation.definitionFit: The black art is sorcery or witchcraft, the practice of casting magic charms on people.
